Stated Claim / Post Context:
Edinburgh University is cutting the very subjects that define Scotland

I’VE had my shield up for universities for months now, since Andy Burnham – graduate of Fitzwilliam College, Cambridge – began steering working-class youth away from academic and towards vocational qualifications.

Actual Article Body:
Share

I’VE had my shield up for universities for months now, since Andy Burnham – graduate of Fitzwilliam College, Cambridge – began steering working-class youth away from academic and towards vocational qualifications.

The idea that even one single kid would be discouraged from the joys of abstraction, or the richness of comparison, or any other of the intellectual adventures possible in an academic context… well, my fists are up.

But sometimes – indeed, often these days – universities’ behaviour makes it pretty difficult to defend them. I’ve been looking at the list of 90 degree courses being cut from the arts and humanities schools at Edinburgh University.

The national outrage is the range of Scottish-cultural degrees being discontinued. As a sole or joint subject, it’s five in Celtic, 11 in Scottish Literature and three in a subject I never even knew existed, Scottish Ethnology.

READ MORE: Ann Widdecombe murder suspect charged with planning terror act against Nigel Farage

Some of the conjugations remind me what I love about the universality of a university. You can get degrees in “Law” and Celtic? Scottish Ethnology and “Scandinavian Studies”? “Portuguese” and Scottish Literature?

Some would regard these as supreme indulgences. I would hail it as the kind of internal evolution that happens at a great university, where a community of scholars are free to follow their noses.

But the UoE (University of Edinburgh) management, who are operating under a well-publicised rule of finding £140 million of savings, point to the paltry – sometimes non-existent – student numbers for these Scottish courses.

They’re working to a criteria of viability that mandate at least 30 students for undergraduate programmes (20 for postgraduate programmes), as well as “applicant demand, cost of delivery and associated research income”.

The joint honours degree in English and Scottish Literature – which is not being cut – currently has 31 students and averages nine new entrants annually.

Still, even that seems a poor show, with the standalone degree in Scottish Literature being closed. Across all degree programmes relating to Scot Lit earmarked for closure, there were only 19 students enrolled in total. Out of these programmes, five currently have zero students.

At some point, you have to look at the nature of the demand. More than 70% of students at Edinburgh come from England, the rest of the UK or overseas. They bring their fees with them – but perhaps not automatically an interest in “Scottish studies”.

Last week, it was confirmed that Edinburgh University would close several Scottish literature courses. (Image: Anna Urlapova)

This is where I agree with many recent critics. They want to specify that universities have obligations to their national culture that cannot be measured solely through enrolment and research income.

In this paper, the writer Jim Mackintosh recently sought to raise ambitions for the School of Scottish Studies and its archives – established in 1951 and holding more than 33,000 sound recordings, manuscripts and oral histories.

Jim claims it should be formally recognised and funded as a national intellectual infrastructure for all of Scotland, rather than treated as a routine university asset.

Instead of isolating subjects into tiny single-honours degree tracks, suggests Mackintosh, the university should create a major interdisciplinary hub. One that connects Scottish literature, Celtic, ethnology, oral history, folklore, music, anthropology, archaeology and digital humanities.

This is a reasonable ambition – and it strikes me from two angles, one personal and one technological.

Firstly, I’m someone who had to self-educate themselves in the cultural history of Scotland. I got nothing from my comprehensive education in the 70s, and even less from an English literature and language degree in the eighties.

(Scottish literature was available at the University of Glasgow – but I didn’t even have a minimal backgro
